how: Loop format (Matteo 2026-11-17). One recording per reel. Each loop line = bridge + hook said in ONE breath; the edit starts the reel at the hook and ends it on the bridge, so the replay is the same continuous sentence. Edit here, then run build_loop.py.
intro: Fighter breakdown, episode {ep}. I'm Matteo. I've trained in five countries, and every episode I break down one fighter you can learn from.
cta: Comment PLAN and the fighter you want next, and I'll send you the plan for this one.

reels.title: Mike Tyson
reels.why: Biggest name recognition in the series. The old Tyson plan reel (no breakdown) got under 350 views, so this tests the new shape on the same fighter.
reels.note: Plan exists (tyson-peekaboo). Check: Cus D'Amato's peek-a-boo style, heavyweight champion at twenty.

loops.bridge: So if you're the smaller guy in the room,
loops.hook: Tyson was short for a heavyweight, and he made that his weapon.

loops.bridge: And that's what makes people ask:
loops.hook: Why was Tyson so hard to hit when he was walking straight at you?
Tyson was heavyweight champion at twenty, and it started with his defence.

loops.bridge: And most people miss this part.
loops.hook: Everyone thinks Tyson was just power. Watch his head, not his hands.

loops.bridge: It all goes back to one coach.
loops.hook: Cus D'Amato took a short kid and built a whole style around being short.

body: It's called peek-a-boo, and it's three things.
One. The guard. Gloves on his cheeks, elbows on his ribs. He's the smallest target in the ring.
Two. His head never stops. Side to side, even when nobody's punching. You can't aim at something that's always moving.
The third one is where the power came from.
Three. Every slip loads a punch. Slip to the right and your weight is already on your right leg. Right hand to the body, right uppercut. His defence and his offence were the same move.
So if you're shorter than your sparring partner, move your head first, then punch.

reels.title: Israel Adesanya
reels.why: Competitor outlier: 'Why Israel Adesanya is called The Last Stylebender', 286k views, 39x that channel's normal.
reels.note: Plan NOT written yet (Claude writes it before this posts). Check: long kickboxing career before the UFC. The 'same fake twice' part is a breakdown of how feinting works, so confirm it against a clip before you say it.

loops.hook: Most fighters throw to land. Adesanya throws to learn.
Why does everyone freeze against Adesanya?
Adesanya makes you defend strikes he never throws.
Adesanya's best weapon isn't a strike. It's a twitch.
Adesanya was a kickboxer for years before he ever fought in a cage, and it shows.

body: He's a kickboxer in a cage, and it comes down to three things.
One. The feints. A twitch of the shoulder, the hip, the knee. You react every time, and now he knows how you react.
Two. The distance. He stands one step outside your reach, so you have to walk onto his counter.
The third one is why people freeze.
Three. The same fake, twice. The first time you flinch. The second time it's real, and it lands in the gap you just opened.
So next spar, spend one round only faking. Watch how your partner reacts. That's your map.

reels.title: Khabib Nurmagomedov
reels.why: Adds grappling to the series. No competitor outlier behind it in our data, so it is the control against the strikers.
reels.note: Plan exists (khabib-pressure). Check: retired 29 and 0, wrestled from early childhood under his father.

loops.hook: Everyone knew Khabib was going to shoot. Nobody could stop it.
Why did great strikers look helpless against Khabib?

loops.bridge: And that's how he did it:
loops.hook: Twenty-nine fights, zero losses, and the game plan was three steps.
Khabib's punches weren't there to knock you out. They were there to walk you to the fence.

loops.bridge: It started when he was a kid.
loops.hook: Khabib wrestled from early childhood under his father, and it shows in every fight.

body: Everyone says it's his wrestling. It's how he uses it.
One. He walks you to the fence. His punches aren't there to knock you out. They're there to close the distance.
Two. He never stops at one attempt. The single leg fails, so it becomes a double. That fails, so it's a trip. The next one is already coming.
The third one is why nobody had answers.
Three. He makes you carry him. Once you're down, all his weight is on you. Every second, you're carrying him. You get tired. He doesn't.
So if you grapple, don't fall in love with one takedown. Chain three.

reels.title: Oleksandr Usyk
reels.why: Optional fourth: chosen for style variety and because the plan exists. No competitor outlier behind it, so skip it if you only want three.
reels.note: Plan exists (usyk-balance). Check: southpaw, undisputed cruiserweight, beat Joshua twice and Fury twice.

loops.hook: Usyk beat much bigger men, and he didn't hit harder than them.
How does a cruiserweight beat the biggest men in boxing?
Usyk beat Joshua twice and Fury twice. Here's what he was doing.
Usyk's balance drills look weird. They're the whole fight.
Usyk's training videos look like a dance class, and there's a reason.

body: He's a southpaw, and it comes down to three things.
One. His feet never stop. Small steps, side to side, so a bigger man never gets a still target.
Two. His head stays over his feet. Even moving, he's balanced, so he can punch from any position.
The third one is what those weird drills are for.
Three. He punches on the move. Sideways, backwards, he throws and lands without stopping to set his feet.
So if you're always the smaller one, stop setting your feet. Punch while you move.
